clinicalPearls: Inherited disorder of low apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins, most commonly from heterozygous truncating variants in the APOB gene, producing persistently low LDL cholesterol and apoB.
Heterozygotes are frequently asymptomatic and may be discovered incidentally on a strikingly low LDL cholesterol, often with a mildly favourable cardiovascular profile.
Hepatic steatosis is the principal clinical concern in heterozygotes, because impaired VLDL assembly and export traps triglyceride within hepatocytes.
Homozygous or compound heterozygous disease is severe, resembling abetalipoproteinaemia with fat malabsorption, steatorrhoea and failure to thrive in infancy.
Severe disease causes deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins, leading to spinocerebellar degeneration, peripheral neuropathy, retinitis pigmentosa and acanthocytosis.
Inheritance is co-dominant: gene dosage determines severity, so obligate parents of a severely affected child show intermediate low lipid levels.
Distinguish genetically from PCSK9 loss-of-function hypocholesterolaemia and from acquired causes such as malnutrition, malabsorption, hyperthyroidism and severe liver disease.
In contrast to abetalipoproteinaemia (an MTP-gene recessive disorder), FHBL is usually an APOB defect and heterozygotes still produce some apoB-containing lipoproteins.
reference.pathophysiology: Familial hypobetalipoproteinaemia results from defective production or secretion of apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins. Apolipoprotein B is the structural backbone of chylomicrons, VLDL and LDL; its full-length hepatic form, apoB-100, and the intestinal form, apoB-48, are essential for packaging and exporting dietary and endogenous lipid. Most cases stem from heterozygous variants in APOB that generate truncated apoB proteins which are secreted poorly, degraded rapidly or unable to bind lipid efficiently, so the liver and gut export fewer and smaller triglyceride-rich particles and circulating LDL cholesterol and apoB fall to very low levels. Because triglyceride cannot be exported normally from the hepatocyte, it accumulates within the liver, giving the hepatic steatosis that characterises symptomatic heterozygotes. When both APOB alleles carry loss-of-function variants, apoB output is negligible and the phenotype converges on that of abetalipoproteinaemia: dietary fat cannot be absorbed and transported, producing infantile steatorrhoea, fat malabsorption and failure to thrive, together with profound deficiency of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. Vitamin E deficiency in particular underlies the progressive spinocerebellar and peripheral neurological degeneration and the pigmentary retinopathy, while altered erythrocyte membrane lipid composition produces acanthocytosis. The condition is thus mechanistically distinct from disorders of lipoprotein clearance, being a defect of lipoprotein assembly and secretion rather than catabolism.
additionalDifferentials: Abetalipoproteinaemia due to microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTTP) deficiency
Chylomicron retention disease (Anderson disease) with selective intestinal fat malabsorption
Secondary hypocholesterolaemia from malnutrition, malabsorption or advanced liver disease
Chronic infection or malignancy with low lipid levels
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease from other metabolic causes when steatosis is the presenting feature
additionalInvestigations: Fasting lipid profile with apolipoprotein B, characteristically showing very low LDL cholesterol and apoB
APOB gene sequencing (and MTTP where recessive severe disease suggests abetalipoproteinaemia) with family cascade testing
Fat-soluble vitamin levels, particularly vitamin E, with vitamins A, D and clotting studies for vitamin K status
Liver imaging and liver function tests to detect and quantify hepatic steatosis
Peripheral blood film for acanthocytes in suspected severe disease
Neurological and ophthalmological assessment including retinal examination when deficiency is advanced
Assessment of growth, faecal fat and nutritional status in affected infants
redFlags: Infantile failure to thrive with steatorrhoea suggesting severe biallelic disease
Progressive ataxia, sensory loss or areflexia indicating vitamin E deficiency neuropathy
Visual deterioration or night blindness from retinitis pigmentosa or vitamin A deficiency
Bleeding tendency from vitamin K deficiency and coagulopathy
Signs of advancing chronic liver disease in a patient with longstanding steatosis
reference.prognosis: Heterozygotes generally have a normal lifespan and may enjoy reduced cardiovascular risk, with hepatic steatosis being the main long-term issue requiring monitoring. Severe biallelic disease carries a guarded prognosis dependent on early diagnosis and lifelong high-dose fat-soluble vitamin supplementation to prevent irreversible neurological and retinal damage.
pitfalls: Dismissing a very low LDL cholesterol as benign or laboratory error and missing the underlying diagnosis and its steatosis risk.
Confusing heterozygous FHBL with abetalipoproteinaemia; the inheritance pattern, gene involved and parental lipid levels differ.
Attributing hepatic steatosis solely to metabolic syndrome and overlooking a monogenic lipoprotein-secretion defect.
Failing to initiate and sustain fat-soluble vitamin replacement in severe disease before neurological injury becomes fixed.
Overlooking cascade screening of relatives, who may be silently affected.
